posts.name: Ronway
posts.cooked:
Effects are not consumed, they trigger everytime their condition is met.

In the case of "first time x would be dealt damage each turn", that will trigger everytime it is the first time x would be dealt damage each turn. If somehow a target manages to achieve this twice in the same turn (not sure how, as nothing occurs simultaneously, so whatever happens after the first would have to be the second, followed by third, then fourth, etc.) then that will trigger twice. 

It's even the same case with "next damage dealt" effects. Sure it take the appearance of being consumed, but what is actually going on is the effect has no means to trigger again. As once the "next damage dealt" has been dealt, there will not be another next for the purposes of whatever created the effect in the first place. 

Take effects that occur at the end of a specific turn. Why do we only trigger those once? Not because they are consumed afterwards. It's because they tell you to activate at the end of that turn, which only happens once, as every turn only has one end of turn. This is why Sub-zero Atmosphere can allow the villain end of turn effects trigger twice if it is destroyed before the end of the villain turn. If effects were consumed, only the end of villain turn effects that didn't trigger at the start of the villain turn would trigger at the end.

 

Short answer: Effects are not consumed, they trigger whenever possible.

xKillswitch:

In the case of Haka of Sheilding and Driving Mantis, we saw that even though Fixer had not been dealt damage, the shielding was consumed because it was required in order to trigger the redirect.

Whether or not Fixer actually takes damage has nothing to do with wether or not the "next damage" will be consumed. All modifiers happen at the same time in the damage order sequence: Determine attack type -> determine all modifiers. The game doesn't check to see if it applies before applying the trigger. As soon as the next damage will be dealt, the modifier applies. However, we have a separate rule that sometimes, retroactively, things are canceled. So, in the case of a normal redirection, all modifiers are canceled. If it is required for the redirection, then it isn't canceled. This is the reason (and the only reason) why it wouldn't be "consumed". This is exactly what Christopher said, that the reason is because everything is canceled, not because it didn't deal damage. Therefore, "next damage" will always apply the next time damage is being attempted (except when you can't deal damage, then the entire sequence is canceled immediately), and only sometimes will retroactively get canceled (i.e., redirection, prevention, etc.).

Note, that if there isn't a specific effect that cancels it, it will get consumed, even if it had no effect: For example, Stealth gets consumed against irreducible damage, even though it had no effect (nothing cancels it). Haka of Shielding will get consumed in a 1 damage attack with Ta Moko out (nothing is canceling it).

Basically timing of redirection and "first time" wording, with 2 probable resolutions:

A.  Damage would trigger both redirection cards, Guise chooses the order to resolve, the one chosen triggers and resolves, the other does not trigger because Guise is not in a state of being dealt damage.

The second damage triggers the card that failed to trigger and is redirected.

B.  Damage triggers both redirection effects, Guise chooses the order to resolve, the one chosen triggers and resolves, the other one fails, but counts as having been triggered.

The second damage hits Guise.

 

B is my initial choice, but there is arguments for the A

I'm going to rephrase the argument against A. Let's go back to the basics of the game engine. Triggers and Effects.

  1. Both Beefcake and Infiltrate & Obfuscate share the exact same trigger clause. "The first time [Target] would be dealt damage each turn"

  2. When two cards share the exact same trigger clause, if one triggers, then they both trigger. 

  3. Char (Environment target) targets Guise with two instances of 2 damage. When we resolve the first instance of 2 damage, that triggers "The first time [Target] would be dealt damage each turn" clause. Both Beefcake and I&O trigger.

3.A) Guise chooses to resolve Beefcake first, then redirects the damage.

3.B) I&O doesn't have damage to redirect any longer so does nothing.

  1. We start to resolve the second instance of 2 damage.

If A is Correct:

  1. I&O triggers to redirect the second instance of 2 damage.

5.A) I&O can only trigger if it's trigger clause is met.

5.B) If I&O's trigger clause is met, and shares the exact same trigger clause as Beefcake, then it follows that Beefcake must also trigger.

"But I&O wasn't 'consumed', so it can trigger while Beefcake was 'consumed' so it wont"

Ongoing effects are not dictaed by whether they were used or not. They are only dictated by whether their trigger condition is met. 

If you want to argue that I&O triggers on that second instance of damage, then you have to nessesarily argue that the trigger clause for that redirection effect is being met. No way around that.

Now, if we are saying that the second instance of damage is now being considered "The first time" (and it has to be if you want I&O to trigger at all) due to the first redirection reseting the attack, what stops a 3rd instance of damage from also being considered "The first time" after the second redirection? If a first redirection can reset what is considered the "first time you would be dealt damage that turn", why wouldn't the second redirection? Now we have a case where a 3rd instance of damage is also considered "the first time you would be dealt damage that turn", which nessesarily would meet the trigger clause requirments of Beefcake and I&O.

Whether you actually agree or not, you just set yourself up for a solid argument for infinite redirections under this interpretation of the rules.

If B is Correct:

  1. Beefcake and I&O both triggered in step #3, both recognizing that the first instance of 2 damage Guise recieved as "The first time [Target] would be dealt damage each turn". Guise could have resolved either one first in step #3.A remember.

5.A) It now follows that this second instance of 2 damage now must be labled as "The second time [Target] would be dealt damage this turn". 

5.B) The trigger clause for I&O and Beefcake are both considered (both are still active ongoing effects), but can not be met, so neither effect can trigger.

5.C) Guise takes 2 damage

Clean. Simple. Follows all the rules we know about how trigger clauses and effects work. I like it.

This whole debate of "Next" vs "First" I think is 100% pointless.  Ongoing effects are, and have always been, dictated by their trigger clause.

Thank you for pointing out that Next and first, as I have been saying the entire time, differ by their point of activation.

First always requires a start point for tracking.  Like:

The first time today

The first time each turn

The first time ever

Next doesn't, because it starts tracking from the moment you activate the word.  Normally that is by saying the word, in this game it is by activating the effect that is tied to "Next".  You would accomplish this by using a power that uses next, or playing a card that uses next.

The reason First is used in the card game is for effets that reset, and can happen once per turn/round, but not multiple times inside that time period.

Next is used for effects that don't reset, and only trigger once per use of the effect.

But once you say/activate "Next" it starts tracking, and the first occurance of the event you are looking for will be the event that is "Next."  At that point Next is done, the effect is over, and will not trigger until the effect that uses next is activated again, by using a power, incap, playing a card, etc.

 

The second instance is the "next" instance after the first instance. You telling me that is not correct use of the word next?

The second instance is the "first" instance after the previous instance. You telling me that is not correct use of the word first?

 

When you restart the tracking you restart the effect.  You can't just reapply an effect in this game because you want to, Haka of Battle requires the card to be played, and directions followed.  As soon as that card is played tracking begins, and it looks for the next damage, not 1 of the next 2 damages.

posts.name: phantaskippy
posts.cooked:
Reassess is not reapply.

Let me spell out my thoughts again and see if this clears up what I am saying:

DW Setback uses Mitigate

Tachyon plays Synaptic Interruption.

Villain A tries to deal Tachyon 5 damage.

Mitigate and Synaptic both trigger.

Mitigate reduces it by 2, Synaptic redirects the damage.  We know from the ruling that Mitigate is not consumed, it is still active.

 

But the Next time a hero would be dealt damage has occurred, and has passed.  The window of triggering Mitigate is over.

The only way for that not to be true is:

1.  Redirection restarts a very specific set of effects, without requiring the cost to be paid again, and only if their application was not needed for the redirection.

-or-

2.  The "would be dealt" status is cancelled, and treated as if no hero would have been dealt damage by the attack that was redirected. (assuming the redirection was to a non-hero)  The effect of Synaptic is not undone, because it was needed for the redirection to occur.

 

I am firmly in camp #2.

The last time we had rules start getting this crazy ended in Christopher changing order of operations to be player choice outside of Start and End of turn effects.

When you start having to account for things like "did the reduction say first or next, and was the initial damage prevented or redirected or reduced to 0, and did reduction matter to the redirection or prevention?" I start to think this is not the intent of the game, and the answer is something far simpler.

That's why I think the most effective way to resolve this is to have a simple question for Next/first.

Has the target been dealt damage this turn?  If no then this is the first time the target would be dealt damage this turn.

or

Has the target been dealt damage since Haka of Battle was played?  If no, then it is the next time that target has been dealt damage.

 

It is simple, it is elegant, and it removes the fiddliness.

posts.cooked:
I definitely don’t want to restart the definition argument, but I also want to keep this on top of the forums so it gets noticed. :-)

One thing I wanted to note was it seems people are taking Christopher's ruling on Driving Mantis/Shielding to mean that modifiers are always applied first.  That is not how I took it.  I took it as an extension of “the players choose the order of events”.  I think this applies broadly to the First vs Next debate.  I like to think of it like it is in the App.  When damage is applied, a box comes up with all the cards that “could” trigger from this event and you choose the first to use.  If you choose a redirect, nothing else happens.  If you choose a modifier, if there is still damage left it gives you the same options minus the one you chose.  You could then select a redirect, and both are used.  So the order you choose them in has more of an effect that the working on the cards.  I think it is the same with multiple redirects.  Like with Beefcake and I/O, if the environment deals him damage, that same box comes up (in my mind) with all the cards that could possibly trigger off that damage.  You select what you want to use.  They both redirect the damage, so the second doesn’t trigger.  If he gets damaged again by the environment in the same turn, the 2 redirection cards would not apply because it is no longer the first time he was damaged.  If he had Shielding/Stealth on him, those would come up as possible effects in the list, but if you don’t choose them, they will keep showing up until they have to be used because you can’t prevent/reduce the damage dealt.

Hope this makes sense.

posts.name: Killswitch
posts.cooked: Just to clarify, the Mantis/Shielding ruling had nothing to do with modifiers being applied first or not. The ruling was that one-time modifiers like Haka of Shielding are used up when they are necessarily applied in cases where they get redirected, but the damage value was necessary for the redirection to occur in the first place. So with Driving Mantis, we see that Fixer must redirect instances of 2 or less damage. Shielding will take the damage down to 1, and gets redirected. Even though damage modifications are re-calculated, Shielding is not re-calculated because it was necessary for Mantis to redirect it, and it can only be used once.

posts.name: AlexxKay
posts.cooked:
AvatarX:

I like to think of it like it is in the App.  When damage is applied, a box comes up with all the cards that “could” trigger from this event and you choose the first to use.  If you choose a redirect, nothing else happens.  If you choose a modifier, if there is still damage left it gives you the same options minus the one you chose.

This is not strictly true.  The App presents you with all the effects that could trigger during a particular timing subphase.  Damage Prevention and Redirection effects share a subphase, but this definitely happens before effects that modify the damage Amount.  (For a detailed list of subphases as we currently unerstand them, see this google doc.)

One example where this subphase breakdown can be easily seen in the App is when Twist the Ether is in play, and there are other effects which could change both the Type and Amount.  The Type effects get chosen/resolved first, and only then do you choose the order of Amount effects.
